source_contract.statement: Subscription creation is rejected before mutation when the current user cannot read the skill metadata.
Published and yanked subscriber fan-out selects recipients using event-time current access facts before dispatch.
All skill visibility decisions for this change are made by VisibilityChecker; the batch resolver contains no independent authorization branch.
Private, namespace-only, hidden, removed-member and disabled-user each have explicit subscribe and fan-out assertions, and denial text resolves in English and Chinese.
VisibilityChecker currently owns hidden, latest-version, visibility, namespace-role and SUPER_ADMIN decisions and has eight production call sites.
Account-active and archived-namespace inputs belong in a new full-context VisibilityChecker overload while existing overloads and their eight callers remain behavior-compatible.

No migration, prune, historical subscription cleanup, subscription-count repair or /me/subscriptions redesign is included.
No confirmPublish, event producer, event record, workflow or public PR mutation is included.

invariants.statement: Subscribe and fan-out proceed only when the shared checker grants current metadata read access.
Missing or non-active accounts are denied before subscription or recipient effects, including disabled SUPER_ADMIN.
Unauthorized private, hidden and stale-member actors reach no subscription mutation and no recipient-visible notification sink.
Denied subscribe performs no row write, counter increment or event; an allowed non-idempotent subscribe performs all three once.
Losing metadata read access never prevents a user from deleting their existing own subscription.
Unsubscribe decrements exactly when an existing row is deleted and is a no-op for an absent row.
isSubscribed preserves the authenticated caller's own relationship boolean and anonymous false behavior pending maintainer choice.
Fan-out uses account, membership and role facts loaded at event handling time, never a subscription-time snapshot.
Each fan-out performs at most one batch lookup per account, namespace-member and platform-role source and no such lookup inside the candidate loop.
Any authoritative eligibility lookup or async admission failure occurs before every recipient persistence and transport sink.
Published fan-out skips the publisher and yanked fan-out skips the actor even when the checker grants access.
Yanking the last published version does not create a wasPublished bypass; latestVersionId null remains owner-only under VisibilityChecker.
The eight existing VisibilityChecker call sites retain their overloads and observable access, masking and payload behavior.
Subscriber listeners run through the configured async Spring proxy only after a successful transaction commit; rollback produces no sink.
Reflection, generated, external and runtime-conditional surfaces remain explicit audit evidence rather than being treated as absent.

work_partition.no_split_rationale: The checker interface, subscribe guard, batch resolver and both fan-out paths share one authorization matrix and exact-sink fixtures; splitting would couple signatures and fixtures across lanes and create more merge risk than schedule benefit.

declined_lenses.reason: This change has no replicated log, partitioned data or cross-node derived record; the concrete local after-commit and async ordering surface is covered by the Lamport-style lens.
Interface growth is constrained to one full-context overload and one policy-free resolver; executable RED and final-sink sensitivity has more material review value for the third seat.

members.rationale: subscription-create and both subscriber fan-out paths protect PRIVATE_METADATA_CONFIDENTIALITY and ACCOUNT_STATUS_FAIL_CLOSED while stale rows survive, so an attacker-shaped review must challenge role priority and every recipient sink.
must_answer: Can an active or disabled SUPER_ADMIN exploit account-versus-role ordering to bypass subscription-create or either fan-out path?
Can removed-member or stale-row state reach published-notification-row, yanked-notification-row, or either SSE sink?
Does SubscriberAccessResolver contain any allow or deny branch outside VisibilityChecker, including hidden, latest-null, archived or role comparisons?
Under what concrete condition is this plan wrong, and can an attacker construct a counterexample that still passes the ten named scenario assertions?

members.rationale: spring-runtime-dispatch and FAIL_CLOSED_BEFORE_SINK depend on transaction commit, current fact reads and asynchronous scheduling before recipient persistence, so ordering errors can invalidate otherwise correct visibility logic.
must_answer: Does transaction rollback produce strictly zero notification rows and SSE pushes through the real Spring proxy?
Are account, membership and platform-role facts read after commit at handling time rather than captured at subscription or publication time?
Can any account, namespace, membership or role batch failure create a prefix of recipient rows before the failure?
What observable state remains when the executor rejects or the async listener throws, and is any such state incorrectly reported as successful fan-out?

members.rationale: the ten R4 assertions, visibility-checker-consumer-regression and final NotificationService/SSE sinks must distinguish the insecure base from the candidate without replacing the production path with mocks.
must_answer: Do private, hidden, removed-member and disabled-user probes fail on the base for the intended unauthorized mutation or dispatch rather than for missing test scaffolding?
Do fan-out probes execute a real NotificationDispatcher and assert recipient-specific NotificationService rows plus matching SSE payloads?
Does the no-N-plus-one probe count actual account, membership and platform-role repository calls and prove zero calls inside the candidate loop?
Can the eight-consumer regression and latest-null yank probe kill an implementation that changes old overloads or reintroduces a wasPublished bypass?
